title: Felix and the Bridge
premise: In the final winter of a continental war, Hazel Almeida drives for suffragist Miriam Vance, secretly reading every letter he carries and keeping his own ledger of names — the disappeared, the requisitioned, the executed. When the army occupies their river town and seizes the town's official records to bury a massacre on the old bridge, Hazel realizes his private ledger is now the only true account that exists. Racing the armistice negotiations, he must smuggle the ledger across occupied lines to a neutral journalist, choosing between safety and testimony. The book ends days before the armistice: Hazel delivers a copy to the press at terrible personal cost, loses the bridge and nearly his life, but wins the only victory available to him — the names survive in print, outliving the victors' historians.
about_author: Elodie Reyes is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated wartime records in provincial repositories. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: What Fits in a Satchel
chapters.summary: Hazel Almeida, driver and letter-reader, introduces his habit of memorizing what he carries and measuring his life by portability. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking loneliness; the reader learns he trusts paper more than people.

chapters.title: Mrs. Vance's Correspondence
chapters.summary: Miriam Vance dictates fiery letters for the suffrage circuit while Hazel steers through mud and checkpoints. He reads one meant for a widow and says nothing. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: the first crack — knowledge as burden rather than privilege.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Hazel reveals his private ledger of names: men taken by patrols, letters never delivered, a boy conscripted at fifteen. POV: Hazel, with a flashback to its first entry. Emotional beat: complicity turning into purpose.

chapters.title: Orders Come Down
chapters.summary: The army announces it will requisition the town: billets, grain, horses, and all municipal records 'for audit.' The mayor complies with trembling gratitude. POV: Hazel observing the town square. Emotional beat: dread arriving politely, in triplicate.

chapters.title: The Bridge at Dusk
chapters.summary: Hazel witnesses soldiers sealing the old bridge after dark and hears shots he cannot account for. In the morning the army posts a notice about 'bandit activity.' POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: horror compressed into inference; he writes three new names.

chapters.title: A Letter He Shouldn't Have Read
chapters.summary: Among Mrs. Vance's mail, Hazel finds an order routing the seized ledgers to army headquarters for destruction. He copies it word for word. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: the moment invisibility becomes impossible — he is now evidence.

chapters.title: The Widow Okafor
chapters.summary: Hazel delivers a condolence letter to a woman whose son was on the bridge; she already knows, from a survivor's whisper. She asks him to remember her boy's full name correctly. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: grief demanding precision; memory becomes a duty owed person by person.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Soldiers take the livery stable, the flour store, and finally Mrs. Vance's motorcar papers. Hazel negotiates to keep the car 'in service' by driving officers. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: humiliation weaponized — access purchased with servility.

chapters.title: Inside the Commandant's House
chapters.summary: Driving for Captain Brandt, Hazel sees the confiscated town ledgers stacked in a parlor, awaiting burning. He notes which clerk handles them and when. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: cold clarity; fear transmuted into reconnaissance.

chapters.title: Mrs. Vance Suspects
chapters.summary: Vance catches Hazel copying documents and confronts him; instead of betrayal, she offers the suffrage network's courier routes as cover. POV: alternating Hazel and Vance. Emotional beat: alliance forged between two people who trust no one.

chapters.title: The Neutral Correspondent
chapters.summary: Through the network, they contact Ruth Ellery, a journalist stranded at the Grand Hotel awaiting the armistice. She agrees to take testimony — if it can reach her before the victors sign and seal the record. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: hope with a deadline.

chapters.title: Checkpoint at Mill Road
chapters.summary: A test run of the route fails; a courier is detained and the network goes silent. Hazel burns his first draft of testimony. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: the price of survival made literal — someone else paid it.

chapters.title: Brandt's Dinner Party
chapters.summary: Ordered to drive officers to a celebration of the coming armistice, Hazel serves wine to the men who sealed the bridge and listens as they joke about 'the paperwork problem.' POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: rage held perfectly still.

chapters.title: The Clerk Who Kept Copies
chapters.summary: A junior army clerk, sickened by the burn order, slips Hazel a duplicate page list of the bridge dead — then vanishes. POV: Hazel, with the clerk's note reproduced. Emotional beat: unexpected grace; proof arrives from inside the machine.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Hazel walks the riverbank below the bridge at night and finds what the water returned. He records descriptions, not just names. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: mourning fused with method; the ledger becomes testimony.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Choir Loft
chapters.summary: A network member breaks under interrogation; soldiers raid a safe house where the testimony was being typed. The typist escapes with half the pages. POV: the typist, then Hazel. Emotional beat: rising panic — the clock and the net are both closing.

chapters.title: Armistice Rumors
chapters.summary: Word spreads that signing may come within days — or be delayed indefinitely. Brandt orders the remaining ledgers burned tomorrow morning. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: desperation sharpened into decision; there will be no second chance.

chapters.title: The Crossing
chapters.summary: Hazel hides the ledger and the clerk's pages in the spare tire well and drives Brandt himself toward the hotel, betting the captain won't search his own chauffeur. At a checkpoint he talks his way through using the officer's name. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: white-knuckle climax of nerve; survival and truth riding in the same vehicle.

chapters.title: Testimony at the Grand Hotel
chapters.summary: In Room 214, Hazel reads the ledger aloud while Ellery types; Vance corroborates; the widow Okafor identifies her son. Brandt's aide arrives hunting a stolen ledger and finds nothing but a chauffeur waiting with the car. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: catharsis — the truth spoken on the record, witnessed.

chapters.title: The Burning of the Records
chapters.summary: That night the army burns the town ledgers in the square; Hazel watches his neighbors watch, understanding that everything he carried is now the only copy. Brandt suspects him but has no proof — and no time. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: solemn triumph shadowed by danger.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Hour
chapters.summary: Ellery's dispatch wires out hours before the armistice takes effect; bells ring; soldiers become men again overnight. Brandt detains Hazel briefly, then releases him — the war is over, and killing a chauffeur solves nothing now. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: release without absolution.

chapters.title: Names That Outlast the Bridge
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Ellery's article runs with the full list of names; the widow Okafor reads hers aloud at a memorial on the ruined bridge. Hazel begins a new ledger — this time of survivors. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: resolution — justice outside the law achieved as memory made public; he is visible at last, and unafraid.
